# Identity, equality, and hashing

robjc provides several ways to compare objects.
Choose one according to the question you want to answer.

| Question | Method | Basis for the result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Do two references point to the same instance? | `identical()`, `==`, `!=` | Object identity |
| Should two objects count as equal values? | `$isEqual(other)` | Equality defined by the class |
| Where should a Set element or Dictionary key be sought? | `$hash()` and `$isEqual(other)` | Narrow candidates by hash, then check equality |

`hash()` does not decide equality directly.
Distinct objects may have the same hash.
This guide first separates identity from equality, then implements both `isEqual()` and `hash()` in a custom class.

## Compare identity with `identical()`, `==`, and `!=`

robjc instances are reference objects.
Assigning one to another variable makes both variables refer to the same instance.
Creating another instance with the same value produces a **different object**.
robjc distinguishes **equality as values** from **identity as one object**.

For robjc objects, `==` and `!=` compare **identity** using `identical()`.

```{r}
library(robjc)

first   <- RSNumber$new(7L)
alias   <- first
another <- RSNumber$new(7L)

stopifnot(identical(first, alias))
stopifnot(first == alias)
stopifnot(first != another)
stopifnot(!identical(first, another))
```

`first` and `another` wrap the same integer and are **equal as values**, but they are separately created instances.
**`==` checks identity rather than the wrapped value**, so it is `FALSE` for this pair.

## Compare values with `isEqual()`

Each class can define what it means for two objects to be equal as values through `isEqual()`.
For example, `RSNumber` inherits value comparison from `RSScalar`; it returns `TRUE` for separate instances that wrap equal values.

```{r}
stopifnot(first$isEqual(another))
stopifnot(another$isEqual(first))
stopifnot(first == alias)
stopifnot(!(first == another))
```

To compare values in a custom class, define `isEqual()`.
The following `Label` class regards separately created instances as equal when they hold the same string.

```{r}
Label <- RSObjectClass(
  "GuideEqualLabel",
  private = list(.text = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(text) {
      super$initialize()
      if (!is.character(text) || length(text) != 1L || is.na(text))
        stop("`text` must be one non-missing string.")
      private$.text <- text
      invisible(self)
    },
    text = function() private$.text,
    isEqual = function(other) {
      if (!robjc_isInstance(other) || !other$isMemberOf(self$class()))
        return(FALSE)
      identical(private$.text, other$text())
    }
  )
)

label_a <- Label$new("ready")
label_b <- Label$new("ready")
label_c <- Label$new("done")
stopifnot(label_a$isEqual(label_b))
stopifnot(!label_a$isEqual(label_c))
stopifnot(!label_a$isEqual(RSString$new("ready")))
stopifnot(label_a != label_b)
```

The method first checks that `other` is a robjc instance and a direct member of the same class as `self`.
It can then return `FALSE` for `NULL` or a different kind of object without calling `other$text()`.
Once the class check succeeds, it compares the strings returned by `text()` with `identical()`.
`label_a$isEqual(label_b)` is `TRUE`, but `label_a == label_b` is `FALSE` because the instances are distinct.

When defining `isEqual()`, preserve reflexivity (an object equals itself), symmetry (if `a` equals `b`, then `b` equals `a`), and transitivity (if `a` equals `b` and `b` equals `c`, then `a` equals `c`).
Set and Dictionary lookup depend on this consistency.

## Understand the `RSObject` defaults

`RSObject$isEqual()` uses `identical(self, other)`.
Without an override, an object is equal only to itself.

```{r}
left <- RSObject$new()
right <- RSObject$new()
stopifnot(left$isEqual(left))
stopifnot(!left$isEqual(right))
stopifnot(is.integer(left$hash()), length(left$hash()) == 1L)
stopifnot(!is.na(left$hash()))
```

The default `hash()` derives an integer from the instance's environment address, but that integer could be `NA_integer_`.
It passes the result through `robjc_normalize_hash()`, which maps `NA_integer_` to `0L`.

An address based hash is useful for lookup within the current R session.
It is not guaranteed to stay the same across sessions or to be unique among all instances.
Classes such as `RSScalar` that compare by value override both `isEqual()` and `hash()`.

## Look up objects in Set and Dictionary

Set uses an object's `hash()` and `isEqual()` to detect duplicates and test membership; Dictionary uses them to look up keys.
A separate instance can find a stored element when the two are equal and have the same hash.

In a linear search, code walks through elements from the start and compares each with `isEqual()`.
The number of comparisons grows with the collection; finding the last element or a missing one requires checking them all.
robjc Set and Dictionary use hash tables instead.
They place elements or keys according to `hash()` when inserting them.
During lookup, they calculate the search object's hash and call `isEqual()` only on candidates in the corresponding location.

If hashes are well distributed, average lookup time stays roughly constant as the collection grows.
If many objects share a hash, more candidates must be compared.
A hash narrows the search; it is not a unique object identifier.

Equal objects must return the same hash.
The reverse does not hold: sharing a hash does not imply equality.
`isEqual()` distinguishes candidates whose hashes collide.

```{r}
set <- RSMutableSet$new()
set$addObject(RSString$new("apple"))
set$addObject(RSString$new("apple"))
stopifnot(set$count() == 1L)
stopifnot(set$containsObject(RSString$new("apple")))

dictionary <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
dictionary$setObjectForKey(RSNumber$new(3L), RSString$new("quantity"))
stopifnot(identical(
  dictionary$objectForKey(RSString$new("quantity"))$value(), 3L
))
```

## Implement custom equality and hashing

The next class holds one integer as a key.
It considers instances with the same integer equal and calculates a hash from that integer.
`value()` is read-only so the key value cannot change after insertion into a Set or Dictionary.

For ordinary hash calculations, use the shared `RSHashOperator$instance`.
Its `hashForScalar()` calculates hashes for length-one R values such as `integer` and `character`; `computeHashCodeWithString()` handles strings specifically.
For arguments and calculation details, see the class documentation with `help("RSHashOperator", package = "robjc")`.

```{r}
operator <- RSHashOperator$instance
stopifnot(is.integer(operator$hashForScalar(12L)))
stopifnot(identical(
  operator$hashForScalar("apple"),
  operator$computeHashCodeWithString("apple")
))
```

The `NumberKey` example deliberately uses a simple remainder calculation to show hash collisions and the role of `isEqual()`.
For a real class, consider `RSHashOperator` according to the value being hashed.

```{r}
NumberKey <- RSObjectClass(
  "GuideNumberKey",
  private = list(.value = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(value) {
      super$initialize()
      if (!is.integer(value) || length(value) != 1L)
        stop("`value` must be one integer.")
      private$.value <- value
      invisible(self)
    },
    value = function() private$.value,
    isEqual = function(other) {
      robjc_isInstance(other) &&
        other$isMemberOf(self$class()) &&
        identical(private$.value, other$value())
    },
    hash = function() {
      computed_hash <- as.integer(private$.value %% 10L)
      robjc_normalize_hash(computed_hash)
    }
  )
)

a <- NumberKey$new(12L)
b <- NumberKey$new(12L)
c <- NumberKey$new(22L)
stopifnot(a$isEqual(b), identical(a$hash(), b$hash()))
stopifnot(!a$isEqual(c), identical(a$hash(), c$hash()))
```

Here, the hashes of `12L` and `22L` deliberately collide.
Because `isEqual()` compares their full values, Set and Dictionary can still treat them as separate elements and keys.

```{r}
keys <- RSMutableSet$new()
keys$addObject(a)
keys$addObject(b)
keys$addObject(c)
stopifnot(keys$count() == 2L)
stopifnot(keys$containsObject(NumberKey$new(12L)))
stopifnot(keys$containsObject(NumberKey$new(22L)))

lookup <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
lookup$setObjectForKey(RSString$new("twelve"), a)
lookup$setObjectForKey(RSString$new("twenty-two"), c)
stopifnot(identical(lookup$objectForKey(b)$value(), "twelve"))
stopifnot(identical(
  lookup$objectForKey(NumberKey$new(22L))$value(), "twenty-two"
))
```

At the **end** of a custom `hash()` method, return `robjc_normalize_hash(computed_hash)`.
If an integer calculation produces `NA_integer_`, this function replaces it with `0L`.
Returning `NA_integer_` directly would make the hash unusable for collection lookup.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(robjc_normalize_hash(NA_integer_), 0L))
stopifnot(identical(robjc_normalize_hash(42L), 42L))
```

Normalization does not automatically make equality and hashing consistent.
Your implementation must ensure that **if `a$isEqual(b)` is `TRUE`, then `a$hash()` and `b$hash()` are equal**.
While an object is stored as a Set element or Dictionary key, do not change the state that determines its equality or hash.
Dictionary calls `copy()` on a key when inserting it.
See the [collections guide](guide_07_Collections.Rmd) for Dictionary usage.
